Volume 11 · Chapter 11

Financial crises and systemic mechanisms

Advanced Author-reviewed · Prerequisites: v11-c10

By the endTrace balance-sheet feedback, runs and contagion in a crisis model.

Trace a crisis through decisions, prices and payment dates

Capability. Derive a small run game with endogenous sale prices, identify its equilibria without inventing a selection probability, and follow the losses and cash through a contracted creditor network. Compare a funded liquidity line with a resolution stay, stating who supplies money, who receives it and who bears the remaining risk. The prerequisite is financial regulation and incentives; the dated liquidity, operational and stress-accounting distinctions in Chapter 5, Chapter 6 and Chapter 7 remain essential.

A bank can own assets sufficient to repay patient creditors and still face a run. Sales made to meet early demands can depress the very price used to assess its equity. A creditor bank can then miss its own payment even when some recovery will arrive tomorrow. A promise of support changes this mechanism only if its timing, funding and repayment terms are credible. These are distinct propositions; an alarming balance-sheet picture alone proves none of them.

1. Specify the institutions before solving the crisis

Alder and Beacon are fictional institutions in one currency, CU. There are two cutoffs, 1 and 2. Cash held across the cutoffs earns zero. Assets produce no cash before cutoff 2. Everyone in the benchmark game knows the contracts and the terminal asset payoff of 1 per unit. There is no private information, risk aversion or uncertainty in that game. Later stress states change the terminal payoff on an already fixed cutoff-1 history; they are not assigned probabilities.

Opening positions immediately before the funding choices
EntityAssetsPrincipal claims and equity
AlderUsable cash 20; 100 long assets initially marked at 1Retail payment 18 due at cutoff 1; two funders with principal 31 each; debt 20 to Beacon due at cutoff 1; equity 20
BeaconNo cash; the 20 claim on AlderCustomer obligation 10 due at cutoff 1; equity 10
Public lending vehiclePrepositioned taxpayer cash 80Taxpayer-owned equity 80; no unmodeled borrowing

Alder's opening identity is 20+100=18+2(31)+20+20. Each of the two strategic funders simultaneously chooses R, requesting principal 31 at cutoff 1, or W, replacing that right with a promise of 34.1 at cutoff 2. The waiting premium is 3.1 per funder. Funders maximize total consumption at cutoff 2, storing any earlier receipt; utility is linear. They are two large decision makers, not a continuum of depositors. The retail 18 is an exogenous early payment, not a third strategic player.

The following payment rules are part of the original example. At cutoff 1 Alder first pays retail, then requesting funders pro rata, then Beacon. A short payment remains an unpaid claim; it does not disappear. At cutoff 2 any public loan is senior on Alder's remaining estate. The waiting promises and unpaid runner or Beacon claims then share the residual estate pro rata. Shareholders receive what remains. There is no acceleration, penalty, recovery expense or additional loan. Beacon uses actual receipts to pay its customer, retains cash, and applies later receipts to the still-unpaid obligation. These stipulated priorities are not claims about a jurisdiction's insolvency law.

The public policies below are alternatives. The same 80 CU is not simultaneously assigned to every alternative. The vehicle lends only cash already available before the relevant cutoff; unused cash remains its asset. A central bank can create settlement balances under its own powers and balance-sheet arrangements, but that different financing mechanism is not silently substituted for this vehicle. Neither a promised guarantee nor a debt write-down adds usable cash by itself.

2. Close the sale-price feedback explicitly

Let s be the units Alder sells at cutoff 1. Outside buyers supply a stipulated uniform auction price

p(s)=p0−λs;   sale receipts R(s)=s p(s)=p0s−λs².

All units in the auction sell at that one clearing price. Thus receipts are p(s)s, not the integral under an inverse-demand curve. The buyers acquire the sold assets and receive their terminal payoff. The price schedule is an absorption assumption, not a derived competitive valuation or an empirical estimate. Initially p0=1, λ=1/200 and asset inventory N=100.

The outside buyers bring a separate initial cash endowment p0N, sufficient because 0≤R(s)≤p0N on the allowed domain. Their unused cash remains theirs. It is not Alder's deposit cash or the public vehicle's budget. This completes the funding source of the auction rather than treating a quoted price as a cash receipt without a buyer.

Write c for cash, e for retail, f for each funder's principal, K for the network debt and m∈{0,1,2} for the number of runners. With no public loan, the cash that must be raised to meet all cutoff-1 claims is z=max(e+mf+K−c,0). Here z=18+31m. Alder chooses the smallest sale sufficient to raise z; if that is impossible it sells all available units and applies the stated payment order. This is an imposed liquidation policy, not an optimal-control theorem.

Existence and regime proof. For 0≤s≤S≤N, suppose λ≥0 and 2λN≤p0, with p0>0. Then R is continuous, R(0)=0, and R′(s)=p0−2λs≥0. It is strictly increasing between any two different points of [0,S]: the derivative can vanish only at a single endpoint when λ>0. Hence z≤R(S) has exactly one solution there; z>R(S) cannot be fully funded by sales. At z=R(S), all free units are sold and the budget just closes. For λ>0 the feasible root is

s=(p0−√(p0²−4λz))/(2λ)=2z/[p0+√(p0²−4λz)].

The second expression avoids subtracting nearby numbers. For λ=0, s=z/p0. If z=0, no sale is needed. Outside the monotone domain, a revenue target can have two roots or selling more can raise less cash. Our lab rejects that domain instead of treating full liquidation as a universal funding remedy.

Worked example 1 — Three funding profiles, one auction rule

Without support, maximum sale receipts are 50. The three targets are 18, 49 and 80. The first two fit; the last does not.

No-line outcomes at the benchmark terminal payoff
Runners mUnits soldSale priceCutoff-1 payments: retail/runners/BeaconEach waiting funder at cutoff 2
0200.918 / 0 / 2034.1
1100−10√2 ≈ 85.8578641/2+√2/20 ≈ 0.57071118 / 31 / 2010√2 ≈ 14.142136
21000.518 / 52 / 0No waiter

With no runners, 80 retained units pay 80 at cutoff 2, enough for the two 34.1 promises; shareholder value is 11.8. With one runner, retained assets are 10√2, all paid to the sole waiting funder. With two runners, each receives 26; 10 of their principal and all 20 owed to Beacon remain unpaid, with no later Alder assets to recover. Beacon consequently misses its own 10 payment. A financial link has transmitted a cash failure even though Beacon sold no asset.

3. Solve the run incentives and retain the selection problem

A funder must compare a deviation with the changed auction outcome, not hold the old sale price fixed. If the other waits, waiting gives 34.1 and running gives 31. If the other runs, waiting gives 10√2 and running gives 26. Therefore WW and RR are strict Nash equilibria: neither player gains by a unilateral deviation. RW and WR are not equilibria because the waiter prefers to join the run. These four profiles exhaust pure strategies.

Let x be the probability that the other funder runs in an independent mixed strategy. The expected payoffs are UR(x)=31−5x and UW(x)=34.1−(34.1−10√2)x. Their difference is affine. The unique interior indifference point is

x*=3.1/(29.1−10√2) ≈ 0.207249.

The denominator is positive and greater than 3.1, so x* lies strictly between zero and one. Running is a strict best reply above x*, waiting below it. When both use x*, each is indifferent, so independent randomization gives a symmetric mixed equilibrium. There is no asymmetric nondegenerate mixed equilibrium: each mixing player's opponent must use the same unique indifference probability. A player facing pure W or pure R has a strict best reply, excluding equilibria with only one mixing player.

Worked example 2 — An equilibrium probability is not a measured crisis frequency

At a conjectured other-player run probability 1/10, running gives 30.5; waiting gives 30.69+√2 ≈ 32.104214. Waiting is better. At x=1, the strict preference reverses because 26>10√2. The mixed x* makes the two payoffs equal; it does not tell us which of WW, RR or the mixed equilibrium will be selected in repeated real institutions.

Announcements, beliefs, information, coordination devices and changes in contract enforceability could change behavior. None is a selection mechanism in the present game. Adding a probability to the three equilibria without such a model or evidence would manufacture a forecast. Nor does the toy game establish that all observed withdrawals were irrational: here joining a run is rational against a running counterparty.

4. Separate leverage, loss allocation and physical resources

Before payments, mark the 100 assets at the clearing price q while keeping principal obligations at 100. Alder's marked assets are 20+100q and its equity is E(q)=100q−80. For E>0, the assets/equity ratio is L(q)=(20+100q)/(100q−80), and L′(q)=−10000/(100q−80)²<0. A lower price raises this leverage measure until equity reaches zero; a negative-equity balance sheet does not have a meaningful positive capital leverage ratio.

Initially L=6. At q=.9, prepayment equity is 10 and leverage is 11. Paying 38 of principal reduces cash and debt equally; the retained marked assets are 72, equity remains 10, and postpayment leverage is 7.2. Neither 10 marked equity nor 18 of retained fundamental value minus remaining principal is the later shareholder payment 11.8: waiting interest of 6.2 is still due.

In this calibration zero principal-book equity occurs at q=0.8, hence s=40 and sale receipts 32. The single-runner auction goes beyond that point. More debt or less equity makes small value changes more consequential. A private lender using contemporaneous collateral prices may also reduce lending as prices fall; at an 80% advance rate, 100 unencumbered units marked at .9 support only 72, versus 80 at 1. Forced sales, revised valuations and reduced credit can then reinforce one another. That extra margin-feedback rule would require a new joint clearing problem; it is not secretly solved by our fixed-appraisal public line below.

Do not count the same loss at every institution. Let P1+P2 be Beacon's actual receipts on its 20 claim. Its asset loss 20−P1−P2 is allocated to its shareholders, customers and any supporting public bridge. In the unsupported RR outcome, the 20 asset loss becomes 10 lost Beacon equity plus 10 lost customer claims. Adding all three numbers as distinct system losses would double-count the same impaired claim.

The outside buyer also matters. At terminal unit payoff v, its gain on sold units is G=vs−R(s). Let I be Alder's promised waiting interest, H its final shareholder distribution, Lpriv its unpaid private claims after all recoveries, and Lpub the public loan shortfall. Adding both dated Alder cash budgets yields

E0−H+Lpriv+Lpub=N(p0−v)+I+G.

To verify it, total resources available to Alder's recipients are c+vN+loan−G. Private promised payments are e+2f+K+I; public promised repayment is the loan. Subtract actual payments from promises and use E0=c+Np0−e−2f−K. This establishes the identity without adding Beacon's downstream allocation again. At v=1 the cheap sale transfers value to buyers; the model contains no destruction of the assets' physical payoff. A welfare assessment would need preferences, real disruption or output effects and the cost of public resources, not merely a sum of marked losses.

There is also a consolidated resource check: add the retail and funder receipts, both banks' final shareholder distributions, Beacon's customer receipts, public cash after recoveries and the buyers' final cash plus asset payoff. The total equals the initial cash of Alder, Beacon, the public vehicle and buyers, plus vN. The internal Alder-to-Beacon payment cancels. The lab checks this identity for each line/profile/state and for resolution; unpaid face claims are not additional realized resources.

5. Finance the intervention and assign its downside

Consider alternative public line caps F of 0, 20 and 80. Loans carry zero interest and are repaid first at cutoff 2. The loan uses a fixed appraisal p0 and advance fraction a=.8. Define np=ℓ/(ap0) pledged units and

ℓ=min{max(e+mf+K−c,0), F, ap0N};   S=N−np.

The pledged units cannot also be sold. Apply the earlier auction solution to free inventory S and the remaining target z=max(e+mf+K−c−ℓ,0). The loan is senior over the retained estate; the minimum collateral reservation does not limit its recourse to only the initially earmarked units. This priority, fixed appraisal and permission to lend are explicit hypothetical rights. There is no further within-window margin call, liquidation expense or fee. With different rights or an appraisal that moves with q, both funding and losses must be recomputed.

Worked example 3 — A partial line can protect runners while a creditor misses its cutoff

With cap 20 and two runners, Alder draws 20, reserves 25 units and sells the other 75. The sale price is 5/8 and receipts are 375/8. Cash 20+20+375/8 pays retail 18 and requesting funders 62 in full; only 55/8 reaches Beacon at cutoff 1. Its customer therefore misses 25/8 at that date.

At v=1, the retained 25 repays the public 20 and sends another 5 to Beacon. The network's total recovery is 95/8. Beacon completes its remaining customer payment at cutoff 2 and retains equity 15/8. The later money does not turn the earlier missed payment into timely service. The buyer's gain is 225/8; Alder equity loss 20 plus network claim loss 65/8 equals that transfer.

This RR profile is a contingency, not a benchmark equilibrium under cap 20. With the line, a funder who waits receives 34.1 whether the other waits or runs; running receives 31 in either comparison. With one runner the retained assets are 10√42, and 10√42−20 exceeds 34.1, proving the waiting claim is fully covered. Thus W is strictly dominant. It is still legitimate to stress an off-equilibrium instruction pattern, provided that the assumed pattern is labeled rather than assigned a fabricated likelihood.

Cap 80 eliminates sales in all three profiles. Draws are 18, 49, 80; all original cutoff-1 claims are paid. Waiting is again strictly dominant at v=1. Both caps 20 and 80 consequently have the same benchmark equilibrium WW with actual draw 18. The larger cap is not proved minimal or optimal: its additional promise protects the full-cutoff payment requirement even in the RR contingency.

Hold that full-line RR history fixed and change the cutoff-2 unit payoff to .6. The retained assets now pay 60 against a public claim of 80. Taxpayers lose 20; the vehicle ends with 60 cash. Retail, runners and Beacon already received their contractual cutoff-1 amounts; equity receives nothing at cutoff 2. The line prevented a forced sale and transferred this terminal credit downside to the public balance sheet. If the lower payoff had been known at cutoff 1, the strategic game would have to be recomputed; it cannot simultaneously be treated as an unexpected stress and a known input to the original choices.

6. A stay can preserve assets and interrupt someone else's cash

The separate resolution alternative has stipulated effective authority before cutoff 1. Alder pays retail 18 from cash, retains cash 2 and all 100 assets, stays the funders and Beacon until cutoff 2, and replaces their claims with principal-only pari passu claims of 62 and 20. The waiting premium is cancelled. These changed rights deliberately remove the original run game. No fire sale or new Alder loan occurs. This is a specified restructuring, not a claim that an actual resolution authority can always impose these terms.

Beacon receives nothing at cutoff 1. A stay's preservation of future value supplies none of its 10 needed cash. A separate bridge lends min(10, available public bridge cap) before that cutoff, senior at cutoff 2 against Beacon's estate. Its claim on Alder is not simultaneously pledged to another facility. The public vehicle advances the bridge from its existing cash; no assumed guarantee is counted as money.

Worked example 4 — Resolution losses and a funded continuity bridge

At v=1, Alder has 102 at cutoff 2 against restructured principal 82. Funders receive 62, Beacon 20 and shareholders 20. A timely 10 bridge lets Beacon pay its customer at cutoff 1; Beacon later repays 10 and retains equity 10. Without the bridge its customer instead waits until cutoff 2, despite eventual full recovery.

At v=.6, Alder's estate is 62, giving recovery fraction 31/41. Funders receive 1922/41 and Beacon 620/41. Alder's principal-creditor loss is 20. Beacon repays its 10 bridge and retains 210/41; the vehicle loses nothing in this particular state. If v instead falls to .1, Beacon recovers only 120/41, and the bridge loses 290/41. Seniority changes allocation, not the amount of underlying assets.

The no-loss bridge result at .6 is not a guarantee for all states. Its loss at .1 is borne by taxpayers under the stipulated funding. Nor does replacing a promised 34.1 with 31 cost nothing to a waiting funder: the aggregate cancelled WW premium is 6.2. Compare principal recoveries, previously promised interest, actual payment dates and public commitments separately. A smaller apparent cash commitment can come with changed private rights and unresolved implementation costs.

7. Use the mechanism to ask better empirical questions

The Diamond–Dybvig primary reading introduced in Chapter 1 is further context for liquidity insurance and run incentives. Our two observable strategic funders, uniform auction, priority network and funded vehicle are different constructions; no optimal insurance or general suspension theorem is imported.

In his 2 September 2010 testimony, Bernanke distinguished crisis triggers from vulnerabilities and discussed unstable short-term funding, leverage, haircuts and forced sales. That is a dated participant retrospective, explicitly presented as his own views. It motivates mechanisms to investigate; it does not identify a causal rescue effect or supply Alder's numbers. Its historical legal discussion is not a statement of current powers.

To investigate an actual event, reconstruct contracts, asset holdings, encumbrances, withdrawals, prices and usable receipts at common dates. Distinguish an institution-specific fundamental shock from a market-wide buyer constraint; distinguish anticipation of support from support actually delivered. A correlation between sales and falling prices does not identify which caused which. Rescue recipients are selected under distress, so a simple comparison of their later outcomes with untreated institutions does not isolate the rescue effect. Records of delayed, partial and conditional actions are essential.

The model omits endogenous asset production, entry by new buyers, information acquisition, cross-currency constraints, legal disputes, fiscal distortion and political incentives. A policy that improves the modeled game can still create ex ante risk-taking incentives or fail operationally. Specify those extensions before claiming a complete crisis explanation or a universally best intervention.

8. Reproduce the finite crisis file

Download the original input, standard-library model, full output, four-payload manifest and domain/execution guide. The quiet, nonmutating run(data) evaluates the three runner counts for each alternative cap and then values each fixed history in the declared terminal states. From the downloaded directory run python3 v11-c11-analysis.py, or supply explicit --input and --output. The default run quietly writes the neighboring v11-c11-output.json. The CLI protects input and implementation from direct, symbolic-link and hard-link overwrites, including that default path; validation also runs under -O.

Rational input arithmetic chooses the funding regimes exactly. An 80-digit Decimal calculation evaluates square roots and reports amounts to 40 decimal places. A 10−24 payoff-comparison band marks near-indifference as unresolved: a numerical weak candidate is not proof of an exact Nash indifference. The baseline equilibrium statements above have separate exact analytical proofs. The checker independently brackets sale roots with rational bisection, reconstructs dated estates, tests meaningful changed inputs and verifies the printed numerical anchors. Arithmetic agreement cannot authenticate collateral rights, available public cash or crisis probabilities.

Exercises

  1. A sale and its consequences. With no public line and exactly one runner, derive the sale root, price, retained units, waiting recovery and principal marked equity. Reconcile the two cutoffs. Explain why paying Beacon in full at cutoff 1 does not imply that Alder can pay the waiting promise.
  2. Complete equilibrium argument. Derive the four funder payoff pairs, find every pure equilibrium and the symmetric mixed equilibrium, and rule out an equilibrium with only one mixer. At an other-player run probability of 1/10, compare the two expected payoffs. Explain what evidence is missing from a claim that x* is an observed run frequency.
  3. Leverage and different equity concepts. Derive the price derivative of prepayment assets/equity while equity is positive. Compute initial leverage, prepayment and postpayment leverage at q=.9, and the sale/receipt boundary at zero principal-book equity. Reconcile the .9 marked equity with terminal shareholder value under WW.
  4. A line with a remaining payment gap. For cap 20 and RR, compute pledged/free units, auction proceeds, each cutoff's network receipt, Beacon's early customer shortfall and terminal equity at v=1. Reconcile the buyer's gain with Alder and Beacon loss allocation without double counting. Is RR a benchmark equilibrium under this line?
  5. Support is funded and exposed. Show why cap 80 yields no sale in every profile and waiting strictly dominates at v=1. Compare actual WW drawings under caps 20 and 80. Then keep full-line RR actions fixed and set v=.6: compute public repayment/loss/cash, private receipts and equity. Identify what changes if the downside is known before the choices.
  6. Resolution timing and loss bearers. Derive Alder's and Beacon's outcomes under the stated stay with a timely 10 bridge at v=.6 and v=.1. Include the funders, public losses, cancelled WW premium and the original cutoff-1 customer requirement. Contrast a zero bridge cap at v=1. Does a stay finance continuity?
  7. Where the sale proof fails. Prove existence/uniqueness on the declared monotone domain, including λ=0 and the exact free-inventory boundary. Outside that domain, set p0=1, λ=.01, N=100 and z=20. Find both roots, show that selling all 100 raises zero, and explain why the lab rejects this parameter set rather than applying its existing full-sale fallback.
  8. Referee a crisis-policy memo. A memo calls the mixed probability an estimated crisis frequency, adds Alder's network shortfall to all downstream losses, treats a stay as cash, and declares the full line optimal because its baseline equilibrium is good. Correct these claims using the case, propose a bounded empirical design/evidence plan, and identify one omitted behavioral or real-resource mechanism that could reverse a policy ranking.
Complete solutions and evaluation criteria

  1. The target is 49. Solve s−s²/200=49: (s−100)²=200, hence the admissible root is 100−10√2. Price is 1/2+√2/20 and retained units are 10√2. Cash 20+49 pays retail 18, the runner 31 and Beacon 20, leaving zero. The retained payoff 10√2 is below the sole waiting promise 34.1, so it all goes to that funder and shareholders receive zero. Principal marked equity is 100q−80=−30+5√2 ≈ −22.928932. Beacon's earlier full payment follows its place in the cash waterfall and the available sale receipts; it is not a certificate of later solvency.

  2. In the order (player 1, player 2), WW=(34.1,34.1), RW=(31,10√2), WR=(10√2,31), RR=(26,26). Against W, 34.1>31; against R, 26>10√2. Thus exactly WW and RR are pure equilibria. Mixing requires 31−5x=34.1−(34.1−10√2)x, giving the interior x* stated above. Both mixers must face that same probability. A player facing a pure action has a strict preference, so an equilibrium with just one mixer is impossible. At x=1/10, the payoffs are 30.5 and 30.69+√2≈32.104214, favoring W. No selection rule, repeated population or observed calibration has been supplied; neither x* nor its square is an empirical event frequency.

  3. With A=20+100q and E=A−100, differentiating A/E gives (100E−100A)/E²=−10000/E² while E>0. At q=1 leverage is 120/20=6; at .9 it is 110/10=11. Paying 38 reduces marked assets to 72 and principal debt to 62, so equity remains 10 and leverage is 72/10=7.2. E=0 gives q=.8, s=40 and receipts 40(.8)=32. Retained WW assets pay 80 rather than their current mark 72; subtract remaining principal 62 to get 18 fundamental equity before interest, then subtract the 6.2 waiting premium to get 11.8. These are different dated valuation concepts.

  4. The loan 20 reserves 20/.8=25 units. Sale of 75 gives price 5/8 and receipts 375/8. After retail 18 and runners 62, Beacon gets 55/8, leaving 10−55/8=25/8 of its customer payment missed at cutoff 1. Retained payoff 25 first repays the loan 20; the remaining 5 goes to Beacon. Total network recovery is 95/8. Beacon pays its late 25/8 and retains 5−25/8=15/8. Its network asset loss is 20−95/8=65/8, exactly its equity loss 10−15/8; customers eventually recover fully but late. Alder equity loss 20 plus this single network loss 65/8 equals buyer gain 75−375/8=225/8. Adding the network loss again as Beacon equity loss would count the same impairment twice. RR is not an equilibrium: the one-runner retained payoff 10√42, after public repayment 20, exceeds the waiting promise 34.1; running always gives 31, so W is strictly dominant.

  5. Targets 18,49,80 are each within the 80 line cap and collateral advance limit 80, so the respective draws fund the entire target with no sale. In the one-runner comparison, retained payoff 100 repays 49 and can still pay 34.1; WW similarly pays two 34.1 claims after repaying 18. Thus waiting yields 34.1 against either action while running yields 31. Both caps have actual WW draw 18, and neither that equality nor the good equilibrium proves optimality. In the fixed RR downside, 100(.6)=60 repays only 60 of the public 80, a loss of 20 and terminal public cash 60. Retail receives 18, the two runners 31 each and Beacon 20 at cutoff 1; final Alder equity is zero. If .6 is known before choices, recalculate each strategy's recovery and all best replies; it is a different benchmark game, not the old equilibrium with an appended surprise.

  6. At .6, retained cash 2 plus assets 60 yields 62 against restructured claims 82. The fraction is 31/41; funders receive 1922/41, Beacon 620/41, and Alder equity is zero. Beacon's bridge supplies its customer 10 at cutoff 1; its later receipt repays the bridge and leaves 210/41 equity. Public bridge loss is zero in this state. At .1 Alder's estate is 12, giving fraction 6/41; funders receive 372/41, Beacon 120/41. The public bridge loses 10−120/41=290/41, Beacon equity is zero, and customers retain their earlier full payment. The aggregate WW premium cancelled by the changed terms is 6.2 in either state. With bridge cap zero at v=1, Beacon receives nothing at cutoff 1 and misses all 10; it later pays 10 from the 20 recovery and retains 10. The stay preserves future assets but does not finance the earlier service.

  7. Continuity and R(0)=0 give an attained intermediate solution whenever 0≤z≤R(S). For two different sale quantities in [0,S], integrating p0−2λs gives a strictly positive difference under 2λN≤p0; possible zero derivative at the endpoint does not create a flat interval. Hence the solution is unique, including s=S at equality. At λ=0 it is z/p0. For the excluded parameters, .01s²−s+20=0 has roots 50−10√5 and 50+10√5, approximately 27.639320 and 72.360680. Maximum receipts are 25 at s=50; at s=100 they are zero. The old fallback would wrongly equate full liquidation with maximum funding. A different selection rule and capacity test are needed; no general nonmonotone equilibrium theorem was proved.

  8. Illustrative referee response. x* is a strategic indifference probability within a particular two-player game, not an estimate or a selection rule. Consolidate the network claim: its impairment is passed into Beacon equity/customer/public losses, not added to them. A stay changes dates and claims; the separately financed bridge produces usable money. Cap 20 and cap 80 both have strict WW with actual draw 18, while their off-equilibrium payment performance and credit exposures differ. Fixed-history downside losses and cancelled private rights must enter the comparison. No cost of taxation, broader output disruption or ex ante risk choice has been modeled.

    Request timestamped holdings/encumbrances, withdrawal and settlement records, contract priorities, support commitments versus actual disbursements, sale prices/quantities and recipient-selection criteria. Define the outcome and horizon before comparing treated and untreated institutions; address reverse causality and nonrandom rescue selection. A policy discontinuity, eligible comparison population or defensible instrument would need its own identification argument rather than being declared valid by name. For example, anticipated support could encourage future leverage, or a late missed payment could destroy operating output; either extension can change a ranking.

    Rubric, 10 points. Award two each for equilibrium/selection distinctions, consolidated loss accounting, explicit dates/funding/rights, a scoped empirical evidence and identification plan, and an economically meaningful omitted mechanism with its directional reasoning. Accept different supported proposals. A claim of universal optimality, invented legal authority or empirical calibration cannot earn its corresponding domain points.

Teach-back and delayed retention

Teach-back. Explain why support can remove a benchmark run equilibrium while leaving credit risk and implementation questions. Answer outline: compare a funder's changed deviation payoff, identify committed versus drawn funds and unsold pledged assets, then allocate an adverse terminal payoff through senior claims. A good equilibrium does not prove all off-equilibrium payments, actual funding availability, legal powers or a welfare optimum.

Delayed check. (1) Set auction impact λ to zero while retaining the original contracts and v=1. What happens to the run incentives without public lending? (2) In the unsupported RR case, can one add Alder's 20 network impairment to Beacon's 10 equity loss and 10 customer loss? (3) Does a resolution promise received after cutoff 1 repair that cutoff's missed customer payment? Answers: (1) assets sell at 1; targets 18,49,80 all fit inventory. Retained units 82,51,20 cover waiting promises whenever there are waiters. Running gives 31, waiting 34.1, so W is strictly dominant; this is a changed absorption assumption, not a universal claim about liquid markets. (2) No: 20=10+10 is one loss allocation. (3) No: a later remedy can fund a later payment, while the original miss remains in the record.

Sources and the next decision

The scoped 1983 run reading and 2010 US testimony provide method and historical context. All Alder–Beacon numbers, contracts, auction rules, proofs and exercises are original. The next chapter, risk governance and institutional integration, asks who may rely on such a model, which limits bind, and what evidence must accompany an institution's decision.

Sources and further study

  • Douglas W. Diamond and Philip H. Dybvig — Bank Runs, Deposit Insurance, and Liquidity, Journal of Political Economy 91(3), 401–419 (June 1983) — Primary source for private liquidity needs, sequential random service, mutual residual claims and post-deposit run best replies. Original utility, calibration and proof in the chapter establish only the stated feasible insurance comparison and two post-deposit equilibria; no optimal-insurance or policy theorem is imported.
  • Ben S. Bernanke (2 September 2010), Causes of the Recent Financial and Economic Crisis — testimony to the Financial Crisis Inquiry Commission — Participant retrospective distinction between housing-loss triggers and funding/leverage vulnerabilities, collateral haircuts and forced sales, dollar funding mismatch and different intervention instruments during the U.S. 2007–09 crisis.
